questions.prompt: A patient with a stomach acid–reducing drug gets more foodborne infections. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The drug blocks histamine release from gastric mast cells
Gastric juice (pH ~2) normally destroys swallowed microbes
The drug kills the S. epidermidis that protects the gut
The drug destroys the ciliary escalator in the trachea

questions.explanation: The stomach is the end point for mucus swallowed from the airway and eyes.

why.A: Acid reducers don't affect mast cells this way.

questions.prompt: Whooping cough's tracheal cytotoxin progressively destroys the ciliary escalator (slides). What problem would follow?

options.text: Mucus and trapped microbes pile up, causing violent coughing
Skin pH rises because sebum production in the airway drops
Gastric acid production stops because less mucus is swallowed
Tears stop draining through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose

questions.explanation: Without cilia, coughing is the only way to clear mucus.

why.C: Gastric acid doesn't depend on swallowed mucus.

questions.prompt: Which statement comparing defenses is FALSE?

options.text: Starfish have both nonspecific and specific defenses.
Fever does not get better with repeated infections.
Adaptive defenses improve with repeated exposure.
Only vertebrates have specific (adaptive) defenses.
Innate defenses are present from birth.

questions.explanation: Metchnikoff's starfish only have nonspecific defenses.

questions.prompt: A blood pressure reading can hint that an internal infection is under way. Why?

options.text: Bacteria consume blood, so the total blood volume drops
Neutrophils constrict the vessels near the infection site
Pus collects in the vessels and raises the blood pressure
Histamine-driven vasodilation during inflammation lowers BP

questions.prompt: In which order do events occur after a splinter carries bacteria into the skin?

options.text: Pus forms → histamine → mast cells release → redness → WBCs exit → healing
Histamine → vasodilation → leaky vessels → WBCs exit → phagocytosis → pus → healing
Abscess → splinter → WBCs exit → vasodilation → histamine → pus → healing
Phagocytosis → histamine → vasodilation → leaky vessels → injury → pus → healing

questions.prompt: Which pairing of first-line defense and mechanism is INCORRECT?

options.text: Earwax — digests peptidoglycan with HCl
Sebum — lowers skin pH
Tears — flush the eye and contain lysozyme
Mucus — traps microbes

questions.explanation: Earwax is acidic from sebum/fatty acids; HCl is in gastric juice.

why.C: Correct — tears flush and contain lysozyme.

questions.prompt: Neutrophils arrive first, but macrophages ultimately clear more bacteria. What explains this pattern?

options.text: Macrophages arrive first but wait for neutrophils before they start eating
Neutrophils don't do phagocytosis; they only release histamine at the site
Neutrophils eat at once but die; monocytes must first become macrophages
Macrophages only eat pus, so they can keep going after neutrophils stop

questions.prompt: A drug blocks the fusion of lysosomes with phagosomes. Which step of phagocytosis fails?

options.text: Extension of pseudopods around the microbe
Digestion of the microbe in a phagolysosome
Binding of the microbe through Toll-like receptors
Release of histamine from nearby mast cells

questions.explanation: No lysosome fusion means no hydrolytic enzymes reach the microbe.

questions.prompt: Why might a person with a weakened sense of 'search, recognize, destroy' (slides) get infections from normally harmless microbes?

options.text: Their skin becomes too acidic, killing the S. epidermidis on it
Their mast cells release far too much histamine all the time
Their normal flora disappear because of the immune changes
Their immune cells fail to tell self from non-self and destroy invaders

questions.explanation: The three mandates of the immune system are surveillance, recognition, and destruction.

questions.prompt: Which two antimicrobial fluids share sebum as a key ingredient?

options.text: Vaginal secretions and sweat
Gastric juice and urine
Skin secretions and earwax
Saliva and tears

questions.explanation: Both are acidic (pH ~3–5) because of fatty acids.

questions.prompt: Which defense would an antihistamine most directly reduce?

options.text: The redness, heat, and swelling of inflammation
The acidity of the gastric juice in the stomach
The lysozyme present in tears and saliva
The beating of the cilia in the trachea

questions.explanation: Histamine triggers vasodilation and leaky vessels.

why.B: Antihistamines don't change stomach acid in this course.

questions.prompt: Why is the inflammatory response described as a 'bridge' between nonspecific and specific defenses?

options.text: It only happens in vertebrates, which are the only animals with immunity
It only occurs after a vaccination has trained the immune system
It is carried out mainly by B cells and the antibodies they make
Histamine can be released after damage or in response to complement and antibodies

questions.explanation: Antibodies (specific) and complement can also trigger it.

why.C: It's run by mast cells and phagocytes.

questions.prompt: Metchnikoff drank buttermilk daily. Which modern concept did he found, and which organism was he relying on?

options.text: Antibiotics; Penicillium
Probiotics; S. epidermidis
Probiotics; Lactobacillus acidophilus
Vaccination; Lactobacillus acidophilus

questions.explanation: He linked a long-lived dairy village to good bacteria.

why.A: Penicillium is antibiotics, not his idea.

questions.prompt: Explain how intact skin uses at least four features to prevent infection.
questions.explanation: It is dry (little moisture), salty (sweat residue), acidic (sebum fatty acids, pH ~3–5, denatures enzymes), and constantly shedding (removes attached microbes), and it carries S. epidermidis that outcompetes pathogens like S. aureus.

questions.prompt: Describe what pus and an abscess are, and how the site is cleaned up and healed.
questions.explanation: Pus is dead neutrophils, phagocytic waste, and tissue fluid; an abscess is the clotted, walled-off site containing the infection and pus. Macrophages engulf the pus and debris, the abscess scabs over, and tissue heals — small sites leave no trace, large ones may scar.
